Green hydrogen is increasingly seen as a critical tool for global decarbonisation, particularly in hard-to-abate sectors. But for developing countries, the question is not only whether green hydrogen can reduce emissions. The deeper question is: how can navigating the green hydrogen transition also drive development? 

Can it expand energy access, create decent jobs, support industrial upgrading, strengthen local value chains, and deliver long-term prosperity rather than simply creating a new export commodity?
 
On Thursday, 14 May, I will be joining Amir Lebdioui , Karim Elgendy and Tinhinan El Kadi at the University of Oxford for the launch of our UNDP-TIDE paper, “Navigating the Currents of Green Hydrogen: Towards a Human-Centred Framework.”
 
The panel will explore how green hydrogen strategies can be designed around a People, Planet and Prosperity framework, ensuring that emerging investments do not reproduce extractive models, but instead strengthen domestic capabilities and sustainable development pathways.
 
I look forward to a rich discussion at the Oxford Department of International Development on the opportunities, risks and policy choices shaping the future of green hydrogen in the Global South.
